```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
```

## Problem 1

### Section 1

```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

Do some data cleaning first. 
Give appropriate units for tmax (°C), tmin (°C), precipitation (mm), and snowfall (mm). 
```{r}
ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  ) |> 
  drop_na(tmax, tmin)
```


Create separate variables for year, month, and day. 
```{r}
ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-",
    remove = FALSE,
    convert = TRUE
  )
```

For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?
```{r}
snow_common =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |> 
  slice(1) |> 
  pull(snow)
```

The most commonly observed values for snowfall is `r snow_common` mm, because most days have no snowfall, even during the winter months.

### Section 2

Calculate the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years.
```{r}
jan_july_temp =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years.
```{r}
ggplot(
  jan_july_temp,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = mean_tmax,
    group = id
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~month,
    ncol = 2,
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      `1` = "January",
      `7` = "July"
    ))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )
```

There is a clear seasonal pattern in average maximum temperature. The average maximum temperature in July is around `r round(mean(jan_july_temp$mean_tmax[jan_july_temp$month == 7], na.rm = TRUE), 1)` °C, which is much higher than the January average of around `r round(mean(jan_july_temp$mean_tmax[jan_july_temp$month == 1], na.rm = TRUE), 1)` °C. Temperatures vary across stations and years, but there is no obvious overall temporal trend. There are a few unusually low January station-year averages below -10 °C, and one particularly low July observation around 14–15 °C, and those unusually obervations can be considered as outliers.


Make a two-panel plot showing 
(i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset
```{r}
tmax_tmin_plot =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = tmin,
      y = tmax
    )
  ) +
  geom_bin_2d() +
  labs(
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature"
  )
```

(ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}
snow_plot =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = snow,
      group = year
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)",
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year"
  ) 
```

Combine these two plots:
```{r, fig.width=16, fig.height=7}
tmax_tmin_plot + snow_plot
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a clear positive association. Snowfall distributions are relatively similar across years, with most nonzero snowfall values below about 50 mm and a smaller number of higher observations.

## Problem 2

### Section 1

Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets.
```{r}
nhanes_covar_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()
```

```{r}
nhanes_accel_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_accel.csv"
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity",
    names_prefix = "min"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute)
  )
```

Merge the two datasets together
```{r}
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_accel_df |>
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar_df,
    by = "seqn"
  )
```


Include:
1. all originally observed variables
2. exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data
3. encode data with reasonable variable classes
```{r}
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
```

### Section 2

Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education Level", "Male", "Female"),
    caption = "Number of Participants by Sex and Education Level"
  )
```

Create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. 
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = sex,
      y = age,
      fill = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Male" = "lightblue",
      "Female" = "#FFD1DF"
    ) 
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

Comment on these items: 
The age distributions for men and women are fairly similar in the less-than-high-school and more-than-high-school education groups. In the high-school-equivalent group, women tend to be older than men, with a noticeably higher median age. Participants with more than a high-school education also appear younger overall than those in the other education categories.

### Section 3

Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. 
Aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. 
```{r}
nhanes_total_activity =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. 
```{r}
nhanes_total_activity |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = total_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Male" = "lightblue",
      "Female" = "lightpink"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity",
    color = "Sex",
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education Level"
  )
```

Comment on your plot:
Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all education groups. Women tend to have higher total activity than men in the high-school-equivalent and more-than-high-school groups, especially at younger and middle ages. In the less-than-high-school group, the difference between men and women is smaller, and both show a clear decline in activity at older ages.

### Section 3
Calculate the average activity at each minute for each sex and education group
```{r}
nhanes_activity_time =
  nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    hour = minute / 60
  ) |>
  group_by(education, sex, hour) |>
  summarize(
    mean_activity = mean(activity)
  )
```

Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. 
```{r}
nhanes_activity_time |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = hour,
      y = mean_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Male" = "lightblue",
      "Female" = "lightpink"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Mean Activity",
    color = "Sex",
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education Level"
  )
```

Conclusion:
Activity is lowest during the early morning hours, increases rapidly after about 5–6 AM, peaks around late morning to early afternoon, and then gradually declines through the evening. The overall 24-hour pattern is similar across all three education groups. Women generally show higher daytime activity than men, especially in the high-school-equivalent and more-than-high-school groups. In the less-than-high-school group, the male and female activity patterns are more similar, although women have a slightly higher peak around midday.

## Problem 3

### Section 1

Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset
```{r}
jan_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

jan_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )

citi_df =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020,
    july_2020,
    jan_2024,
    july_2024
  )
```

The combined Citi Bike dataset contains `r nrow(citi_df)` rides and `r ncol(citi_df)` variables from January and July of 2020 and 2024. Each observation represents one Citi Bike ride. Key variables include ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting and ending station, rider membership status, year, and month. The four datasets were imported separately, variables for year and month were added based on the source file, and the datasets were combined into a single tidy dataset.

### Section 2

Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members.
```{r}
ride_table =
  citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member"),
    caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Status"
  )
```

The number of rides increased from 2020 to 2024 for both members and casual riders. In both years, ridership was higher in July than in January. Citi Bike members consistently had more rides than casual riders, with the highest number of rides occurring among members in July 2024.

### Section 3

Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.
```{r}
top5_stations =
  citi_df |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    sort = TRUE
  ) |>
  head(5) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting Station", "Number of Rides"),
    caption = "Five Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```

### Section 4

Fix the order of plot first
```{r}
citi_df =
  citi_df |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )
```


Calculate the median ride duration
```{r}
median_ride_df =
  citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. 

```{r}
median_ride_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = factor(year),
      group = year
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~month) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year",
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year"
  ) +
   scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2020" = "lightblue",
      "2024" = "lightpink"
    )
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Median ride duration was consistently longer in July than in January and was higher in 2020 than in 2024. Weekend rides, especially on Saturday and Sunday, tended to have longer median durations than weekday rides, with the largest difference observed in July 2020. Overall, ride durations appear to vary by season, year, and day of the week.

### Section 5

For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. 
```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = member_casual,
      y = duration,
      fill = rideable_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~month) +
  labs(
    x = "Membership Status",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type",
    title = "Ride Duration in 2024 by Month, Membership Status, and Bike Type"
  )
```
Ride durations were generally longer for casual riders than for members, and rides tended to be longer in July than in January. Among casual riders, classic-bike rides were typically longer than electric-bike rides. For members, the difference between bike types was smaller, although electric-bike rides tended to be slightly longer, especially in July. All groups show right-skewed ride-duration distributions with a number of unusually long rides.
